extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, legislators, students and readers of political philosophy and law
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Mill's liberty principles to decide when society or law may legitimately interfere with individual conduct, distinguishing self-regarding acts from acts that harm others and giving practical tests and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary maxim: non-accountability for self-regarding actions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The individual is not accountable to society for his actions, in so far as these concern the interests of no person but himself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society may express dislike only by advice, instruction, persuasion, and avoidance. It should not subject such conduct to social or legal punishment. Examples/anti-patterns: majority opinion and public censure are inappropriate grounds to coerce conduct that affects only the actor; imposition of personal tastes as law is illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary maxim: accountability for other-regarding actions
rubrics_metrics.description: "For such actions as are prejudicial to the interests of others, the individual is accountable, and may be subjected either to social or to legal punishment, if society is of opinion that the one or the other is requisite for its protection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conduct harms others, interference by society (social sanction or legal punishment) can be justified to protect those interests. Guidance includes assessing whether the conduct actually injures others and whether punishment or social measures are necessary for protection. Examples: fraud, force, and treachery are modes of success that society properly forbids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish self-regarding from social (other-regarding) actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of conduct as "self-regarding" or "social" determines whether public authority has jurisdiction: trade and actions affecting others are social acts; private tastes and purely personal habits are self-regarding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this distinction to decide if regulation is appropriate. For social acts (e.g., trade, selling goods) society may intervene to prevent fraud, protect public health, or regulate labor safety; for self-regarding acts (e.g., dietary preferences, religious observances, amusements) interference is generally unjustified. Anti-pattern: treating private habits as social wrongs deserving legal punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damage/probability-of-damage test (necessary but not sufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damage, or probability of damage, to the interests of others can justify interference, but the presence of possible or actual damage does not automatically justify society's intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when others suffer loss or pain as a consequence of someone's pursuit of legitimate goals, society should only interfere when the means employed are contrary to general interest (e.g., fraud, treachery, force) or when intervention is necessary for protection. Examples: competition resulting in disappointment is not a ground for intervention; by contrast, deception or violence is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of regulation of trade and commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade is a social act; sellers who affect public interests may fall within society's jurisdiction. Governments may regulate for public ends (pricing historically, prevention of adulteration, sanitary precautions, protection of workpeople).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use market-regulation to prevent fraud, protect consumers, and safeguard worker safety; avoid controls that effectively make harmless goods unobtainable for buyers (these impinge on buyer liberty). Examples/anti-patterns: proper—regulating adulteration or workplace safety; improper—laws that prohibit buyers from obtaining a commodity (e.g., prohibitions that functionally deny consumption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection to the 'social rights' doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection of the notion that every individual has a vested interest that others shall act exactly as he thinks — described as a doctrine that "ascribes to all mankind a vested interest in each other's moral, intellectual, and even physical perfection, to be defined by each claimant according to his own standard."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims that justify coercion to enforce individual moral standards as 'monstrous' and dangerous — they would justify virtually any infringement on liberty. Anti-pattern: legitimating legislation simply because a majority finds certain private conduct personally offensive or morally wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on preventive police functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Government's preventive function (taking precautions against crime or accident) is legitimate but more liable to abuse than punitive measures and should be applied cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interfere preventively only when there is clear evidence someone is preparing to commit a crime or when immediate danger is certain; avoid broad preventive powers that restrict legitimate freedom on mere conjecture. Example: if one is evidently preparing to commit a crime, interference is permissible; if there is only danger or risk, warn rather than forcibly prevent, unless the person lacks capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for incapacity and immediate danger
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person is a child, delirious, or in a state of excitement or absorption incompatible with full reflection, others may lawfully prevent him from exposing himself to danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where capacity for judgment is absent or significantly impaired, forcible prevention (rather than mere warning) may be justified to protect the individual. Example: pulling someone back from an unsafe bridge when there is no time to warn; contrast with competent adults facing risk where warning suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of religious motives as independent grounds for legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation motivated by the desire to avenge supposed offences against the Deity, or to make people religious, is illegitimate unless it protects the interests of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept religious wrongness as a standalone justification for legal prohibition (e.g., Sabbath-inspired bans on amusements are illegitimate when they aim to impose religious observance); protest legislation whose motive is solely religious. Examples: Sabbatarian legislation and attempts to suppress amusements on religious grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against majority-imposed sumptuary and moral laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Majority feeling and public opinion have no rightful authority to regulate personal expenditure, tastes, or private conduct merely because the majority disapproves (e.g., sumptuary tendencies in democratic societies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of laws or social pressure that effectively act as sumptuary laws or prevent individuals from spending incomes in ways that differ from the majority's preferences. Example: democratic social pressure that makes ostentatious living socially unacceptable should not translate into legal coercion; anti-pattern: moral policing that becomes physical coercion to enforce equal incomes or equal rewards.
